messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Very large number of markers
messages.body_plain:
Unfortunately, the way I've coded things, you have to first calculate the full matrix of pairwise recombination fractions.

It's straightforward what to do, to avoid that, but it would be a bit of work; I'll add it to my "to do" list.

karl

On Oct 30, 2014, at 5:35 PM, Mathias Lorieux <m.lo...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi Karl,
>
> I realize that I was not clear at all, sorry. I am trying to figure out what would be the best way to form linkage groups from a dataset with around 45,000 markers, in a population of the ri self or f2 intercross type (typically 200 individuals). The problem is that our datasets (GBS) usually contain plenty of missing data (ranging from 25 to 65 %), so I can't see how findDupMarkers and find duplicates efficiently.
>
> Also, the markers are not ordered a priori since we don't have a reference genome.
>
> My understanding is that in R/qtl it is necessary to compute the LOD score/recombination fraction matrix before forming the linkage groups. And on my machine (64 bit, 16 GB RAM), this take a so huge amount of RAM that R starts swapping on the hard drive and I expect this to last for ages (I calculated that the LOD/recombination fraction matrix' size would be around 65 GB).
>
> So I was wondering if it would be possible to form the linkage groups without computing the entire matrix, for example, one could compute only the recombination fraction and LOD score for the tested pair of markers.
>
> Does this make sense to you?
>
> Thanks very much for the support.
>
> All the best,
> Mathias
>
>
> Le dimanche 26 octobre 2014 19:52:21 UTC+7, Karl Broman a écrit :
> Your question is a bit too vague to be answered precisely. What exactly are you trying to do? What problems are you having?
>
> How many markers? How many individuals? What sort of cross? How much missing data?
>
> You can use findDupMarkers to identify duplicate markers.
>
> karl
>
>
> On Oct 24, 2014, at 11:43 AM, Mathias Lorieux <m.lo...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > Good morning,
> >
> > I'd like to hear about your strategies to deal with datasets containing very large numbers of markers.
> >
> > One approach is to first eliminate duplicates, but one question I have respectful to that is, if there is plenty of missing data, which strategy to search for duplicates should be adopted?
> >
> > All the best,
> > Mathias

messages.subject: How to get rid of the extra ID phenotype?
messages.subject_clean: How to get rid of the extra ID phenotype?
messages.body_plain:
I got the following question by email, and I thought others might be interested in the question and my response.

karl

----

I have formatted my files into csvsr format, but when I used the read.cross function, I always have one more phenotype which is actually the id number. How should I correct this?
>
>  mydata <- read.cross("csvsr",dir="",genfile="updated_step3_geno.csv",
>                       phefile="pheno_drate_mapped.csv", na.strings=c("-", "NA"),
>                       genotypes=c("A", "B"))
>
----

You could just delete the ID phenotype afterwards:
>
> idcolumn <- grep("id", phenames(mydata))
> mydata$pheno <- mydata$pheno[,-idcolumn]
>

messages.body_plain:
The new function, scantwopermhk, works, at least if you use assumeCondIndep=TRUE:

   data(hyper)
   hyper <- calc.genoprob(hyper, step=2.5)
   hyper <- reduce2grid(hyper)
   out <- scantwopermhk(hyper, assumeCondIndep=TRUE, n.perm=16)

karl

messages.body_plain:
You might also consider the pickMarkerSubset function, which seeks to select a subset of markers with no two markers closer than d cM apart. (But it's not very easy to use.)

Related to this paper: Broman, K. W. and Weber, J. L. (1999) Method for constructing confidently ordered linkage maps.Genet. Epidemiol., 16, 337–343. https://www.biostat.wisc.edu/~kbroman/publications/framework.pdf

karl

messages.subject: Using overlapping Bayes credible interval to determine QTL region
messages.subject_clean: Using overlapping Bayes credible interval to determine QTL region
messages.body_plain:
Hi Karl,

I had phenotypic trait data collected in 5 environments (E). Because data were not homogeneous, so I can't combine data sets and had to run QTL analysis for data from each E individually. I'm only focusing on one chromosome, the marker density is pretty high at ~1cM or less on the chromosome.  I've run scantwo, and the results seemed to indicate two major QTL with LOD >2.5 expressed in at least four of the five E. The two major QTL are about 20cM apart, and had no epistatic interaction.

For both major QTL, the QTL peak shifted about 3 to 5 cM from different E. The confidence intervals were estimated using both 1-LOD and 95% Bayes. Since you stated in your guide book that Bayes intervals have consistent coverage for the true QTL location, I was wondering if I could use the overlapping Bayes credible intervals to declare the likely QTL region. An example is shown below.

Trait	position	LOD	% variation	95% Bayes
2009	91.4	4.61	11.14	89-96.96
2010	85.9	6.47	5.89	85-89
2012	94.5	2.05	5.06	68-136.37
2013_1	91.4	9.25	10.03	90-92
2013_2	94.5	3.99	10.87	90-99

Will I be able to declare the QTL is within the region of 89 to 92cM.

Thanks for your comments.

Chao

messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] Using overlapping Bayes credible interval to determine QTL region
messages.body_plain:
Unfortunately, you can't just take the minimal region. With correlated traits, and because the genotypes are shared, the estimated QTL locations are correlated, and so errors in the intervals are also correlated.

It does seem reasonable to focus on the region from 89-92 cM, but ideally you should use multivariate QTL analysis. It's not possible to use R/qtl for that, but you could look at QTL Cartographer, or take a look at the qtlpvl package (https://github.com/jianan/qtlpvl).

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] rf in cM
messages.body_plain:
There's no direct way to make such a plot, but you could make it yourself with a call to image().

    data(hyper)
    hyper <- est.rf(hyper)
    rf <- pull.rf(hyper, "rf", chr=4)
    map4 <- pull.map(hyper)[[4]]
    image(map4, map4, rf, col=gray((0:256)/256))

But to me, it's not so informative.

If you have a physical map of the markers (in Mbp) as well as the genetic map, you could use the est.recrate function in my R/xoi package to estimate the recombination rate along the chromosome.

  http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/xoi/
  https://github.com/kbroman/xoi

karl

Hi Karl,

I want to let you know that I've run MIM on QTL Cartographer using different model selection methods, and the results came out very similar, if not identical, to the results I've had from using scantwo. It tells me that the major QTL are likely real, and using the overlapping interval as the credible region for the presence of the QTL is probably OK. Since I'm working with one single trait, data sets from different Es do correlate, but that should be different from mapping QTL of different but correlated traits, then we need to adjust trait values to account for correlation. In any case, thanks for your comment.

Chao
